title: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
summary: How Rust's ownership rules, moves, shared and mutable borrows, slices and lifetimes rule out double frees, use after free and data races at compile time, and when to reach for clone, Rc or RefCell.
outcomes: Explain how single ownership and scope-based drop replace malloc/free without a garbage collector
Predict whether an assignment or call moves, copies or borrows a value, and the E0382 it can cause
Apply the shared XOR mutable rule and non-lexical borrow scopes to decide if code compiles
Explain why a lifetime parameter like 'a ties a returned reference to the shorter-lived input
Choose between borrowing, clone, Rc and RefCell for a given sharing pattern

lessons.title: Who frees this memory? Ownership and drop

blocks.md: In C you call `malloc` to get heap memory and `free` to give it back, and the compiler checks neither. Three classic bugs follow: a **leak** (never calling `free`), a **double free** (calling `free` twice on the same pointer), and a **use after free** (reading through a pointer whose memory was already freed). All three come from one question C leaves to the programmer: *who is responsible for freeing this block, and when?*

Garbage-collected languages answer it at run time by tracing which objects are still reachable. Rust answers it at **compile time** with a small set of rules called **ownership**, so there is no collector running and no manual `free`. The Rust Book states the rules in three lines:

1. Each value in Rust has an **owner** (a variable or field that holds it).
2. There can only be one owner at a time.
3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value will be **dropped** (its cleanup code runs and its memory is released).

Take the running example of this course, a growable string. `String` is a small fixed-size header plus a heap buffer. The header has three machine words: a **pointer** to the heap buffer, a **length** (bytes in use) and a **capacity** (bytes reserved in the buffer). On a 64-bit target `std::mem::size_of::<String>()` is 24, i.e. 3 x 8 bytes. The header lives wherever the variable lives (here, on the stack); the text lives on the heap.

blocks.caption: Prints 5 8. There is no free call: the compiler inserts the drop at the closing brace.

blocks.title: One owner, one heap block, freed exactly once

scenes.caption: Before `s` exists there is no header and no heap block. Simplified picture: the allocator's own bookkeeping is not shown.
`String::with_capacity(8)` asks the allocator for 8 bytes. The stack header now holds ptr, len 0, cap 8; `s` is the owner of the heap block.
`push_str("hello")` writes 5 bytes into the existing block. Length becomes 5; capacity stays 8 because the text still fits.
At the closing brace the owner goes out of scope. Rust runs `drop` for the String, which returns the 8-byte block to the allocator. Exactly one free, at a point the compiler chose.

blocks.md: This is the same idea C++ calls RAII: tie a resource's release to the end of an object's scope. The difference in Rust is rule 2. Because a value has exactly one owner, there is exactly one place where it gets dropped, so a double free cannot be written in safe code. The next lesson shows what the compiler does to keep rule 2 true when you assign a String to another variable.

When several owners leave scope together, Rust drops local variables in **reverse order of declaration** (the Rust Reference, Destructors). You can run your own code at that moment by implementing the `Drop` trait (a **trait** is a named set of methods a type can implement, like an interface), which is how files close and locks release automatically.

blocks.title: Drop order at the end of a scope

scenes.caption: Three owners are created in order a, b, c. Nothing has been dropped yet.
At the closing brace the last declared value goes first: `_c` is dropped.
Then `_b`, then `_a`. Reverse order means a value declared later (which might refer to earlier ones) is always cleaned up first.
scenes.output:
drop c
drop b
drop a

blocks.md: Ownership answers C's question *who frees this, and when?* statically: the single owner frees it, at the end of the owner's scope. No `free` calls, no collector.

Ownership is not about the stack versus the heap as such. A `String` header can live on the stack, in a `Vec`, or inside a struct field; wherever it lives, that location is the owner, and the heap block is freed when that owner is dropped.

blocks.question: A function creates `let s = String::from("hi");` and returns normally without doing anything else with `s`. What happens to the heap bytes?
options: They are freed when the function returns, because `s` (the owner) goes out of scope and is dropped
They leak, because there is no explicit free
They are freed later when the garbage collector runs
They stay allocated until the program exits
blocks.explain: Rule 3: when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped, and dropping a String frees its heap buffer. Rust has no tracing garbage collector, and nothing waits until exit.

blocks.question: Three local variables `x`, `y`, `z` (declared in that order) all implement `Drop`. In what order do their `drop` methods run at the end of the block?
options: x, y, z
Unspecified; it depends on the optimizer
z, y, x
blocks.explain: Locals are dropped in reverse order of declaration, as specified in the Rust Reference. This is deterministic, not up to the optimizer.

lessons.title: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1

blocks.md: Ownership says one owner at a time. So what should `let s2 = s1;` do when `s1` is a String? Copying the 24-byte header would leave two headers pointing at the same heap block, and both owners would free it at scope end: the double free from C. Copying the heap bytes too (a **deep copy**) would be safe but could be very expensive, and it would happen silently on every assignment.

blocks.prompt: In C, `char *a = malloc(8); char *b = a; free(a); free(b);` is a double free. Rust compiles `let s1 = String::from("hi"); let s2 = s1;`. What does it do to avoid the same bug?
blocks.reveal: It copies only the 24-byte header (pointer, length, capacity) and then treats **`s1` as no longer valid**. This is called a **move**: ownership of the heap block transfers to `s2`. Only `s2` will drop it, so there is one free. Any later use of `s1` is a compile error, `E0382` (borrow of moved value).

blocks.title: let s2 = s1 moves ownership; clone allocates

scenes.caption: `let s1 = String::from("hi")`: s1 owns heap block A (len 2, cap 2).
`let s2 = s1`: the 3 header words are copied (24 bytes). For a moment two headers point at block A, which is exactly the double-free setup.
So the compiler marks s1 as moved-from. It is never read again and never dropped. Only s2 owns block A, so it is freed once. No heap bytes were copied.
To get two independent strings, write `let s3 = s2.clone();` (the top row now shows s3's header): it allocates block B and copies the bytes. Two owners, two blocks, two frees, all correct.

blocks.md: In the last scene read the top header as `s3`, the result of `let s3 = s2.clone();`. Moves happen in three places, not just `let`: assigning (`let b = a;`), **passing an argument** by value (`take(s)`), and **returning** a value from a function. After `take(s)`, the function parameter owns the string, and it is dropped when `take` returns unless `take` hands it back.

blocks.caption: Checked with rustc: the last line is rejected with E0382.

blocks.md: Why not just deep-copy every time? Cost. A move always copies the fixed-size header, 24 bytes for a String, whatever the text length. A clone copies the header and then allocates and copies every byte of the buffer. For a 1000-byte string that is about 1024 bytes copied plus one allocation.

blocks.title: Bytes copied: move vs clone of a String

scenes.caption: Small strings: move copies the 24-byte header, clone copies the header plus 5 heap bytes (29 B) and also makes an allocation.

Large strings: a move still copies only 24 bytes, while a clone copies 1024. This is why Rust makes moves implicit and cheap and makes clones explicit and visible. Simplified: counts header and payload bytes, not allocator overhead.

blocks.md: Some types never need this machinery. An `i32` is just 4 bytes with no heap part, so copying it is complete and harmless. Such types implement the **`Copy`** trait: assignment duplicates the bits and the original stays usable. Integers, floats, `bool`, `char`, shared references `&T`, and tuples or structs made only of `Copy` parts can be `Copy`. The standard library docs give the limit: any type that implements `Drop` cannot be `Copy`, because it manages a resource beyond its own bytes, and `&mut T` is not `Copy` because a copy would alias a mutable reference.
A move is not a deep copy and not a pointer trick at run time. It is a shallow copy of the value's bytes **plus** a compile-time rule that the source is dead. The heap block never moves.
Assigning, passing, or returning a non-`Copy` value moves it. To keep using the original, either `clone()` it (pay for a copy) or lend it out with a reference (next lesson).

options: None; `drop` is special and can be called twice
`drop(s)`, because the first iteration moves `s` into `drop` and the second iteration uses a moved value
`for _ in 0..2`, because loops cannot capture Strings
blocks.explain: `drop` is an ordinary function taking its argument by value, so the first call moves `s`. The compiler sees the loop can run again and reports E0382 (use of moved value). This is a double free the compiler caught.

blocks.question: You define `struct Meters(f64);` and want `let b = a;` to leave `a` usable. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Add `#[derive(Clone, Copy)]` to `Meters`, since its only field is `Copy`
Implement `Drop` for `Meters` so it is cleaned up properly
Wrap it as `Box<Meters>` so assignment copies the box
blocks.explain: A type can be `Copy` when all its components are `Copy`, and `f64` is. `Copy` requires `Clone` as a supertrait, hence both derives. Implementing `Drop` would make `Copy` impossible, and `Box` is never `Copy`.

lessons.title: Borrowing: many readers or one writer

blocks.md: Moving a String into every function that only wants to read it would be painful: you would have to return it back each time. Rust instead lets you **borrow**. `&s` creates a **shared reference** (also called an immutable borrow): a pointer that lets you read `s` without owning it. `&mut s` creates a **mutable reference**: a pointer that lets you modify `s` without owning it. When a reference goes out of scope nothing is dropped, because it never owned the value.

blocks.caption: A reference is one pointer wide (8 bytes on 64-bit), smaller than the 24-byte String it points to.

blocks.md: Borrowing comes with one rule, quoted from the Rust Book: **at any given time, you can have either one mutable reference or any number of immutable references.** Many readers, or exactly one writer, never both. The Book's motivation is the **data race**, which happens when two or more pointers access the same data at the same time, at least one of them writes, and nothing synchronizes the accesses. The rule makes the first two conditions impossible to combine.

The rule also stops a single-threaded bug that C programmers know well. A `Vec` stores its elements contiguously. When `push` finds the vector full (length equals capacity), it needs a bigger block: the allocator may grow it in place, or allocate a new block, copy the elements over, and free the old one. In the second case any pointer into the old block now dangles.

blocks.title: Why a reference into a Vec blocks push

scenes.caption: `let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];` gives length 3 and capacity 3 (measured). `let first = &v[0];` points into the old block.
`v.push(4)` finds the block full, so it allocates a larger one (capacity 6 here; the growth strategy is not guaranteed) and copies the elements.

The old block is freed. In C, reading `*first` now is a use after free. In Rust the program never gets here: `push` needs `&mut v` while `first` (a shared borrow) is still used, so the compiler reports E0502.

blocks.caption: Rejected by rustc. The Book (ch. 8.1) explains it with exactly this reallocation argument.

blocks.md: How long does a borrow last? Not until the closing brace. A reference's scope runs **from where it is created to the last place it is used**. This is the **non-lexical lifetimes** (NLL) design from RFC 2094, which made the borrow checker reason over the control-flow graph instead of lexical blocks. In the example below, the shared borrows end at the first `println!`, so the later `&mut` borrow does not overlap them.

blocks.code:
let mut s = String::from("hi");   // line 1
let r1 = &s;                       // line 2
let r2 = &s;                       // line 3
println!("{r1} {r2}");             // line 4: last use of r1, r2
let r3 = &mut s;                   // line 5
r3.push_str("!");                  // line 6
println!("{r3}");                  // line 7: prints hi!

blocks.title: Borrows live from creation to last use

scenes.caption: Time axis is source lines. The owner `s` is live for the whole block. r1 and r2 are live from lines 2 and 3 through their last use on line 4.
r3 is created on line 5, after both shared borrows have ended. One writer, no readers at the same time: the program compiles and prints hi!.
Add `println!("{r1}")` on a new line 8. Now r1 stays live through line 8, overlapping r3 from line 5: a reader and a writer at once, so rustc reports E0502 at line 5.

blocks.md: Shared XOR mutable: any number of `&T`, or exactly one `&mut T`, never both at the same point in the program. A borrow is live from creation to last use.

The rule is not "only one reference to a variable per function". Sequential borrows are fine, as are many shared ones. The error only appears when a `&mut` borrow overlaps any other live borrow of the same value.

blocks.question: Which snippet compiles?
options: `let a = &mut s; let b = &mut s; a.push('x'); b.push('y');`
`let a = &s; s.push('x'); println!("{a}");`
`let a = &mut s; a.push('x'); let b = &mut s; b.push('y');`
`let a = &s; let b = &mut s; println!("{a}{b}");`
blocks.explain: In option 3, `a` is last used before `b` is created, so the two mutable borrows do not overlap. Option 1 is E0499 (two live `&mut`). Options 2 and 4 are E0502 (a shared borrow is still used after a mutable one starts).

blocks.question: A colleague says the Vec error is pointless in single-threaded code because no other thread can touch `v`. What is the best reply?
options: They are right; the check only matters with threads
`push` may reallocate and free the old buffer, so `first` could dangle even with one thread
`push` always copies the vector, so `first` becomes stale but still safe to read
blocks.explain: Reallocation frees the old block, so the shared reference could point at freed memory: a use after free with no threads involved. `push` only reallocates when length equals capacity, which is exactly why the danger is easy to miss in testing.

lessons.title: Slices and why references cannot dangle

blocks.md: A **slice** is a reference to a contiguous part of a collection instead of the whole thing. A string slice has type `&str`. Its pointer is a **fat pointer**: two words, a pointer to the first byte and a length, so `size_of::<&str>()` is 16 on 64-bit, compared to 8 for `&String`. Range syntax `&s[start..end]` includes `start` and stops before `end`, so the length is `end - start`.

blocks.prompt: A function `first_word(s: &String) -> usize` returns the index where the first word ends (5 for "hello world"). The caller then calls `s.clear()` and later uses the 5 to slice `s`. What goes wrong, and would the compiler notice?
blocks.reveal: The index 5 is just a number with no connection to `s`. After `s.clear()` the string is empty and slicing `0..5` would panic at run time, and the compiler cannot notice because a `usize` does not borrow anything. Returning a **slice** `&str` instead ties the result to `s` through a borrow, so the same mistake becomes a compile error.

blocks.title: first_word returns a slice that borrows s

scenes.caption: `s = String::from("hello world")`: 11 bytes. The underscore marks the space. `first_word` scans for byte 32 (space) and finds it at index 5.
It returns `&s[0..5]`: a fat pointer (ptr to index 0, len 5). No bytes are copied; the slice points into the String's own buffer.
Calling `s.clear()` needs `&mut s` while `word` (a shared borrow) is still used later. Rust rejects this with E0502, so the slice can never outlive the data it views.

blocks.caption: Taking `&str` (not `&String`) lets the function accept both String slices and string literals.

blocks.md: A string literal like `"hello"` is also a `&str`: a slice pointing into the program binary, valid for the whole run. Its full type is `&'static str`, where `'static` is the lifetime meaning "lives for the entire program".
The opposite mistake is returning a reference to something that dies at the end of the function. In C, returning the address of a local array compiles and dangles. Rust refuses:

scenes.caption: `dangle` creates a local String and tries to hand back a reference to it.
At the closing brace the owner `s` is dropped, so the reference would point at freed memory. The compiler has nothing that outlives the call to tie the reference to, so it stops with E0106.
The fix is to return the owned value. Returning moves ownership to the caller, so nothing is dropped at the end of `no_dangle`.

blocks.md: Prefer `&str` over `&String` and `&[T]` over `&Vec<T>` in parameters. A `&String` coerces to `&str` automatically, so the function becomes strictly more general at no cost.

blocks.question: `let s = String::from("hello world"); let w = &s[6..11];` What does `w` hold?
options: A new heap allocation containing "world"
A pointer to byte 6 and length 11
A copy of the whole String header
A pointer to byte 6 of `s`'s buffer and length 5
blocks.explain: Slices never copy data. The range 6..11 starts at index 6 and stops before 11, so the length is 11 - 6 = 5, which is "world".

blocks.question: Why does returning `&s[0..5]` from `first_word` prevent the clear-then-use bug, when returning the index 5 did not?
options: Slices are copied, so clearing `s` does not affect them
The slice is a borrow of `s`, so any `&mut s` (like `clear`) while it is still used is a compile error
`clear` checks at run time whether slices exist
blocks.explain: The borrow checker tracks the slice as a shared borrow of `s`. `clear` needs a mutable borrow, and shared XOR mutable makes the overlap illegal. There is no run-time check involved.

lessons.title: Lifetimes: tying a returned reference to its inputs

blocks.md: Every reference has a **lifetime**: the region of the program during which it must stay valid. Inside one function the compiler infers lifetimes. Across a function boundary it sometimes cannot, because it does not see the caller. The Book's example is `longest`, which returns whichever of two string slices is longer:

The returned reference comes from `x` or from `y` depending on run-time data, so the signature must say how its validity relates to the inputs. A **lifetime parameter** names that relationship. Writing `<'a>` and annotating all three references with `'a` says: the result is valid for a region in which *both* inputs are valid. When the caller passes concrete references, `'a` becomes the **smaller** (overlapping part) of their two lifetimes.

Lifetime annotations do not change how long anything lives. They describe relationships between references so the borrow checker can verify each call site. The function body is checked against the signature, and callers are checked against the signature alone.
Now use it with two strings of different scopes. `s1` is "long string is long" (19 bytes) and lives for all of `main`. `s2` is "xyz" (3 bytes) and lives only inside an inner block.

blocks.code:
let s1 = String::from("long string is long");  // line 1
let result;                                     // line 2
{                                               // line 3
    let s2 = String::from("xyz");               // line 4
    result = longest(s1.as_str(), s2.as_str()); // line 5
}                                               // line 6: s2 dropped
println!("{result}");                           // line 7

blocks.prompt: At run time `longest` would return `s1` (19 > 3), and `s1` is still alive on line 7. Does this compile?
blocks.reveal: **No.** rustc reports E0597: `s2` does not live long enough. The compiler does not run `len()`; it only knows from the signature that `result` is valid for `'a`, the smaller of the two input lifetimes. That is `s2`'s, which ends on line 6, but `result` is used on line 7. Moving the `println!` inside the inner block makes it compile and print the long string.

blocks.title: 'a is the overlap of the input lifetimes

scenes.caption: Axis is source lines. `s1` is valid from line 1 to the end; `s2` only from line 4 until it is dropped at line 6.
At the call on line 5, `'a` must fit inside both input lifetimes, so it can extend at most to line 6, where `s2` dies.
`result` is used on line 7, outside `'a`. The use is not covered, so rustc reports E0597 even though the value actually returned is s1.
Fix: move the `println!` into the inner block (line 5.5 here). The use now lies inside `'a`, and the program compiles and prints the long string.

blocks.md:
Most signatures need no annotations thanks to **lifetime elision**, three rules from the Rust Reference that the compiler applies to fill in lifetimes:

1. Each elided lifetime in the parameters becomes a distinct lifetime parameter.
2. If there is exactly one input lifetime, it is assigned to all elided output lifetimes.
3. In methods, if the receiver is `&self` or `&mut self`, its lifetime is assigned to all elided output lifetimes.

`first_word(s: &str) -> &str` has one input, so rule 2 fills in the output. `longest` has two inputs and no `self`, so no rule applies and you must annotate.

blocks.question: Which signature compiles **without** explicit lifetime annotations?
options: `fn pick(a: &str, b: &str) -> &str`
`fn make() -> &str`
`fn get(&self, key: &str) -> &str` (a method)
blocks.explain: Rule 3: the output takes the lifetime of `&self`. Options 1 and 4 have two input lifetimes and no receiver, and option 2 has no input lifetime at all, so elision cannot fill in the output in any of them (E0106).

blocks.question: A struct holds a borrowed field: `struct Parser<'a> { input: &'a str }`. What does the `'a` promise?
options: The `Parser` lives for the whole program
The `input` string is copied into the `Parser`
A `Parser` value cannot outlive the string data that `input` borrows
The `Parser` owns the string and will drop it
blocks.explain: A lifetime parameter on a struct ties the struct's validity to the borrowed data. The struct does not own the string, and nothing is copied. The checker rejects any use of the `Parser` after the borrowed string is dropped.

lessons.title: When the checker says no: clone, Rc and RefCell

blocks.md: The borrow checker is **conservative**: it accepts only programs it can prove safe, so some correct programs are rejected (the `longest` example showed one). Rust gives you three kinds of escape route, each trading something away. Knowing which one to reach for is most of everyday Rust.

blocks.title: Choosing a tool when the borrow checker says no

nodes.label:
Need the value in
more than one place

scenes.caption: First choice: borrow. If the user of the value finishes before the owner is dropped, a reference costs nothing at run time and the compiler proves it safe.
If the data is cheap to copy or the copy must outlive the original, `clone()` gives an independent owner. Cost: an allocation and a byte copy.

If several parts of the program must keep the value alive and none is clearly the owner, `Rc<T>` counts owners and drops the value when the count reaches zero. Single-threaded only; values behind it are read-only.
To mutate through shared ownership, put a `RefCell<T>` inside. It enforces shared XOR mutable at run time and panics on a violation instead of refusing to compile.

blocks.md: `Rc<T>` (reference counted) is the Book's tool for values with several owners, such as nodes in a graph. `Rc::clone(&a)` does not deep-copy; it increments a count, and the value is dropped only when the count reaches zero. The Book notes it is for single-threaded scenarios only (the thread-safe version is `Arc<T>`). `Rc` only hands out shared access.

`RefCell<T>` provides **interior mutability**: you can mutate the inner value through a shared reference. The rules are the same (one mutable borrow or many shared ones) but they are checked at run time; per the Book, if you break them the program panics. The Book's summary: `Box<T>` allows shared or mutable borrows checked at compile time, `Rc<T>` allows only shared borrows checked at compile time, and `RefCell<T>` allows shared or mutable borrows checked at run time.

blocks.caption: The same aliasing bug as the Vec example, moved from a compile error to a run-time panic.

blocks.md: `clone()` everywhere and `Rc<RefCell<T>>` everywhere make errors go away but give up what ownership buys you: clones cost time and memory, and `RefCell` turns compile-time guarantees into run-time panics. Reach for them when the data really has no single owner, not to silence the checker.

Where this matters in practice: because the compiler knows each value's single owner and every live borrow, safe Rust has no use after free, no double free and no data races, with no garbage collector. The rules also shape API design: functions take `&str` or `&[T]` when they only read, `&mut T` when they modify, and an owned `T` when they keep the value. A signature therefore documents what a function does with its arguments.
Default to borrowing; move when the callee should keep the value; clone when copies are cheap or necessary; use `Rc`/`RefCell` only for data with genuinely shared ownership.

blocks.question: A tree where each child needs a pointer back to its parent, and nodes are created and removed while the program runs. Which choice fits best?
options: Plain `&Node` references stored in each child
`Rc` from parent to children and `Weak` from child to parent (with `RefCell` where nodes must change)
Clone the parent into each child
blocks.explain: Nodes have no single owner whose scope covers every use, which is what plain references need. Cloning would give each child a separate copy rather than the real parent. `Rc` counts owners; a `Weak` back-pointer does not count, so parent and child do not keep each other alive in a cycle that leaks. `RefCell` allows mutation, checked at run time. This is the Book's tree design.

blocks.question: In the RefCell snippet above, what happens?
options: A compile error, E0502
It runs and prints [1, 2, 3, 4]
It compiles, then panics at `borrow_mut` because a shared borrow `r` is still alive
blocks.explain: `RefCell` moves the check to run time. `r` is a live shared borrow, so `borrow_mut` fails and panics. The compiler accepted it because both calls only take `&c`.
